task_1.title: Restore deprecated filename support in send_from_directory
task_1.description: Version 2.0.1 restores backward compatibility for applications calling `send_from_directory` with the older `filename` argument. The renamed `path` argument remains the preferred API, while use of `filename` continues to work with a deprecation warning so existing integrations do not break during the 2.0.x line.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.0.1 does not break existing `send_from_directory` calls that still pass `filename`, while keeping `path` as the preferred argument name and signaling that the old name is deprecated.

expectation.grounded: `send_from_directory` must accept both `path` and the deprecated `filename` parameter. When `filename` is provided, the call should still succeed by treating it as the file path argument and it should emit a `DeprecationWarning`. The `path` parameter remains the documented replacement and should continue to work for current callers.
expectation.conceptual: Applications using the old argument name should keep working after the upgrade, but they should receive a deprecation signal telling them to move to the new argument name. Applications already using the new name should see no behavior change.

constraints.grounded: Do not remove or alter the current `path`-based calling pattern. Preserve `send_from_directory` behavior for normal file serving, and only add compatibility for the deprecated `filename` argument with an observable deprecation warning. If `filename` is supplied, it should be used as the effective path value.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must be backward compatible for older callers without regressing the renamed API. It should add a temporary compatibility layer rather than changing the expected file-serving behavior.

behavior: `send_from_directory` accepts a deprecated `filename` argument again in 2.0.1.
Supplying `filename` causes the function to issue a `DeprecationWarning`.
When `filename` is provided, the file lookup uses that value as the requested path.
Calls that use `path` continue to behave as the primary supported API.
acceptance_criteria: When an application calls `send_from_directory` using `filename=...`, it should return the same file-serving result it would have produced before the rename instead of failing due to an unexpected argument.
When `send_from_directory` is called with `filename=...`, it should emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating that callers should migrate to `path`.
When an application calls `send_from_directory` using `path=...`, it should continue to work without any new warning or behavioral regression.
When both the compatibility argument and the new argument are present, the provided `filename` value should be treated as the effective requested path.

task_3.title: Correct `flask.g` typing for arbitrary attributes
task_3.description: Flask 2.0.1 corrects the public typing of `flask.g` so it is treated as the application globals namespace that supports arbitrary attributes, matching documented usage and preventing false static-analysis failures when applications store custom values on `g`.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Flask 2.0.1 preserves the documented ability to store arbitrary per-context attributes on `flask.g` and eliminates incorrect type-checker or linter complaints about normal `g.some_attribute` usage.

expectation.grounded: `flask.g` should be exposed as an `_AppCtxGlobals` namespace object rather than as an `AppContext`. The public contract should allow arbitrary attribute assignment, lookup, and deletion on `g`, and missing attributes should surface as `AttributeError`. Namespace-style operations such as membership checks and iteration should continue to reflect stored attribute names.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to keep using `flask.g` as a dynamic namespace for request or app-context data, and tooling should understand that this is a supported pattern instead of treating `g` like a fixed-attribute context object.

constraints.grounded: The upgrade must preserve `flask.g` as a local proxy to the globals namespace, continue accepting arbitrary user-defined attribute names, and avoid changing the observable semantics of accessing or deleting absent attributes beyond standard `AttributeError` behavior.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should remove false developer-tooling errors without changing how existing applications interact with `flask.g` at runtime.

behavior: `flask.g` is typed as the globals namespace object instead of the broader application context wrapper.
The globals namespace explicitly supports arbitrary attribute reads, writes, and deletions.
Accessing or deleting a name that is not present on `flask.g` raises `AttributeError`.
Membership checks and iteration on the globals namespace operate over stored attribute names.
acceptance_criteria: When application code assigns a new custom attribute on `flask.g`, the usage should remain valid through the documented attribute-based API.
When static analysis inspects code that assigns arbitrary attributes to `flask.g`, it should recognize `g` as a dynamic namespace object rather than report it as a fixed-slot context object.
When application code reads or deletes an attribute name that has not been set on `flask.g`, it should receive `AttributeError`.
When application code checks for a stored name in `flask.g` or iterates over it, it should observe the names of attributes currently stored in the namespace.

task_2.title: Explicitly export top-level Flask symbols for type checking
task_2.description: The 2.0.1 update makes the public names re-exported from the top-level flask package explicit to static type checkers. This removes false-positive import/export errors in typed user projects while preserving the existing public import surface at runtime.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that public APIs imported from the top-level `flask` package are recognized as explicitly exported by static type checkers, so typed applications can continue using `from flask import ...` without spurious export errors after upgrading.

expectation.grounded: The top-level `flask` package should explicitly export its public re-exports, including names such as `Flask`, `Request`, `Response`, `Blueprint`, `Config`, request/app context helpers, globals like `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session`, helper functions such as `flash`, `send_file`, `url_for`, `render_template`, `render_template_string`, `jsonify`, signal objects, the `json` module, and top-level conveniences such as `abort` and `redirect`. Static analyzers using Flask's bundled typing metadata should accept `from flask import ...` imports for these public names without reporting implicit re-export issues.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to import Flask's documented top-level APIs directly from `flask` and have those imports type-check cleanly with the package's own typing information enabled.

constraints.grounded: The update must preserve the existing public names and runtime import behavior exposed from `flask`; it only changes how those names are declared for typing/export analysis. Existing top-level imports of public symbols should continue to resolve to the same APIs.
constraints.conceptual: This should fix typing/export visibility only, without changing how application code imports or uses the library at runtime.

behavior: Public names re-exported from the top-level `flask` package are treated as explicit exports for type-checking purposes.

Imports such as `from flask import Flask`, `render_template`, `request`, `flash`, and `send_file` remain valid and are no longer flagged as implicit re-exports by static analyzers using Flask's packaged type information.
The top-level package continues to expose the same user-facing API surface, including core classes, helpers, globals, signals, JSON helpers, and the `abort` and `redirect` conveniences.
acceptance_criteria: When a typed application imports public APIs directly from `flask`, static type checking should accept those imports as explicitly exported members of the package.
When a developer imports common top-level names such as `Flask`, `request`, `render_template`, `flash`, or `send_file` from `flask`, the upgrade should not introduce new export-related typing errors.
When existing application code uses the documented top-level `flask` imports at runtime, it should continue to behave the same after upgrading to 2.0.1.

task_4.title: Restore Python 3.6.0 typing compatibility
task_4.description: Version 2.0.1 fixes Flask type annotations and typing aliases that relied on symbols introduced after Python 3.6.0, so supported modules remain importable on that interpreter while preserving equivalent typing semantics for static analysis.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask 2.0.1 remains usable on Python 3.6.0 by avoiding newer standard-library typing symbols that are unavailable on that interpreter, without changing the observable behavior of the affected APIs.

expectation.grounded: Flask should stop requiring runtime availability of typing symbols such as `typing.NoReturn` in `Flask.raise_routing_exception`, `Request.on_json_loading_failed`, and `NullSession._fail`, while preserving their non-returning type contract for type checkers through backported typing support. The `flask.typing` WSGI application alias should also resolve from a typing source that does not depend on modules unavailable in Python 3.6.0.
expectation.conceptual: Type annotations and exported typing helpers should stay compatible with Python 3.6.0. Users on that interpreter should be able to import and use Flask normally, and developers using type checking should still see the same intent and contracts.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the runtime exception behavior or control-flow semantics of routing exception handling, JSON loading failure handling, or null-session mutation failures; only remove dependence on newer typing definitions. Preserve the meaning of the WSGI application typing alias for typing consumers.
constraints.conceptual: This compatibility fix must not alter how the affected APIs behave at runtime. It should only remove interpreter-version-specific typing breakage while keeping the same user-visible outcomes and type meaning.

behavior: Importing Flask modules that define `Flask.raise_routing_exception`, `Request.on_json_loading_failed`, and `NullSession._fail` no longer depends on `typing.NoReturn` being present in the standard library at runtime.
The affected APIs continue to be expressed to type checkers as non-returning call sites through a backported typing definition compatible with older Python versions.
Flask's WSGI application typing alias is sourced from a type-checking definition that remains available for older supported Python versions instead of a newer standard-library typing module.
acceptance_criteria: Given Python 3.6.0, when an application imports Flask components that include routing exception handling, request JSON failure handling, and null-session mutation protection, the import should succeed without failing because a newer typing symbol is missing.
When a developer type-checks code that references `Flask.raise_routing_exception`, `Request.on_json_loading_failed`, or `NullSession._fail`, those APIs should still be treated as non-returning.

When a developer consumes Flask's WSGI application typing alias on supported older Python versions, the type should resolve without depending on a standard-library typing module that is absent on Python 3.6.0.
When these APIs are exercised at runtime, they should keep the same behavioral outcomes as before the upgrade, including continuing to raise rather than return where they previously did.

task_6.title: Reject dotted blueprint identifiers
task_6.description: The patch makes blueprint naming and route registration fail fast when dots are used in identifiers that Flask now treats as reserved for nested blueprint and endpoint resolution. It also keeps blueprint URL rule registration aligned with application rule registration by accepting explicit automatic OPTIONS configuration.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that blueprint configuration rejects dot-containing names and route identifiers so nested blueprint endpoint resolution remains unambiguous, and invalid blueprint registrations fail with explicit runtime errors instead of being silently accepted or relying on assertion behavior.

expectation.grounded: Creating a `flask.Blueprint` with a `name` containing `.` must raise `ValueError`. Calling `Blueprint.add_url_rule` or decorating a route on a blueprint with a custom `endpoint` containing `.` must raise `ValueError`. Registering a blueprint view function whose `__name__` contains `.` must raise `ValueError`. `Blueprint.add_url_rule` must also accept `provide_automatic_options` and pass that setting through to the registered rule.
expectation.conceptual: Blueprint APIs should reserve dots for Flask's own nested blueprint and endpoint naming scheme. If an application tries to use a dot inside a blueprint name, custom endpoint name, or inferred view name for a blueprint route, Flask should reject it immediately with a clear value error. Blueprint route registration should still expose the same observable OPTIONS-handling control that application route registration provides.

constraints.grounded: Blueprints and blueprint routes that use valid identifiers without dots must continue to register normally, including endpoint prefixing behavior used by `url_for`. The new validation must only reject names where dots would conflict with blueprint or endpoint resolution semantics. Passing `provide_automatic_options` through blueprint rule registration must not remove existing blueprint rule options.
constraints.conceptual: Existing valid blueprint setups should keep working unchanged. Only configurations that misuse dot-separated identifiers should now fail early. The fix must preserve normal URL generation and route registration behavior for valid blueprints while keeping explicit OPTIONS handling available.

behavior: A blueprint name containing `.` is rejected at blueprint construction time with `ValueError`.
A custom blueprint route endpoint containing `.` is rejected during blueprint route registration with `ValueError`.
A blueprint view function whose resolved function name contains `.` is rejected during route registration with `ValueError`.
Blueprint URL rule registration accepts `provide_automatic_options` and applies that setting to the resulting route behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When an application creates a blueprint with a dot in its name, it should immediately receive a `ValueError` instead of a usable blueprint object.
When an application registers a blueprint route with a custom endpoint name that contains a dot, the registration should fail with `ValueError`.
When a blueprint route is registered from a view function whose effective function name contains a dot, the registration should fail with `ValueError`.

When a blueprint route is registered with `provide_automatic_options` explicitly set, the resulting route should honor that OPTIONS-handling choice the same way application-level route registration does.
When blueprint names and route identifiers do not contain dots, blueprint registration and endpoint generation should continue to behave normally.

task_5.title: Improve typing for Flask file-serving helpers
task_5.description: Flask 2.0.1 updates the public type contract for its file-serving helpers so typed applications and extensions can use the argument forms the APIs already support, including path-like inputs, binary file objects, optional filenames, timestamp variants, and cache-age callbacks.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask's file-serving APIs expose accurate public typing for supported inputs and optional values so upgrading to 2.0.1 removes false type mismatches around file paths, file objects, cache-age resolution, and optional filename handling.

expectation.grounded: `send_file` should publicly accept filesystem paths, `os.PathLike` values, and binary file objects for `path_or_file`; optional string values for naming and MIME metadata; boolean or string `etag` values; `datetime`, integer, float, or omitted `last_modified` values; and `max_age` as an integer, a callable receiving an optional filename and returning an optional integer, or `None`. `send_from_directory` should publicly accept string or `os.PathLike` values for `directory` and `path`, while exposing an optional `filename` parameter in the callable signature. `Scaffold.get_send_file_max_age` should accept either a filename string or `None` and return either an integer cache lifetime or `None`.
expectation.conceptual: Typed callers should be able to use Flask's file download helpers with the same supported argument forms that the APIs expose at runtime, especially for path-like inputs, binary streams, optional filenames, timestamp values, and computed cache lifetimes.

constraints.grounded: Do not alter the existing response behavior of `send_file` or `send_from_directory`, including attachment handling, conditional responses, cache semantics, or response type. The update should only make the public API contract accurately describe accepted inputs and optional return values for these existing helpers.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must preserve existing file-serving behavior and only clarify the supported API surface for typed consumers; it should not change how downloads, caching, or responses work in normal execution.

behavior: `send_file` publicly identifies `path_or_file` as accepting strings, path-like objects, and binary file objects.
`send_file` publicly identifies `etag` as accepting either a boolean toggle or an explicit string value.
`send_file` publicly identifies `last_modified` as accepting a `datetime`, numeric timestamp, or omission.
`send_file` publicly identifies `max_age` as accepting either a numeric cache lifetime, a callback based on an optional filename, or `None`.
`send_from_directory` publicly identifies `directory` and `path` as accepting string or path-like values and includes an optional `filename` parameter in its callable interface.
`get_send_file_max_age` publicly identifies the filename input as optional and the result as an optional integer cache lifetime.
acceptance_criteria: When a typed application passes a string path, `pathlib.Path`, or binary file object to `send_file`, the public API contract should represent that call as supported.
When a typed application supplies `etag` to `send_file` as either a boolean or a string, the public API contract should represent both forms as supported.
When a typed application supplies `last_modified` to `send_file` as a `datetime`, integer timestamp, float timestamp, or omits it, the public API contract should represent those forms as supported.

When a typed application supplies `max_age` to `send_file` as an integer, as a callable that receives an optional filename and returns an optional integer, or as `None`, the public API contract should represent those forms as supported.
When a typed application calls `send_from_directory` with directory and path values expressed as strings or path-like objects, the public API contract should represent those forms as supported.
When a typed application calls `get_send_file_max_age` with a filename string or `None`, the public API contract should represent an optional integer result.

task_8.title: Restore session availability in custom URL converters
task_8.description: Flask 2.0.1 restores request processing so the session is initialized before URL matching runs. This fixes regressions where custom URL converters and session-backed authentication lookups could fail during route matching because session state was not ready yet.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that requests using custom URL converters can safely access the active session and session-backed user state during route matching, including converters that consult authentication state.

expectation.grounded: Request URL matching must occur only after session initialization has completed, including creation of a null session when the session interface does not return one. Custom URL converters invoked during matching must be able to read `flask.session` and session-backed proxies such as `flask_login.current_user` without failing due to an unset session.
expectation.conceptual: Route matching should run only after per-request session state is ready so custom converters can use session-dependent logic consistently and authenticated requests do not break during parameter conversion.

constraints.grounded: Preserve normal session startup behavior for both real and null sessions, and do not require converter implementations to avoid session access in `to_python`. Because URL matching now happens later, request data derived from matched routing state is not guaranteed to be available during session loading.
constraints.conceptual: Keep session initialization behavior intact while ensuring converter code can rely on session state. At the same time, avoid assuming that route-resolution details already exist before session setup has finished.

behavior: The request context initializes the session before running URL matching.
If session loading produces no session object, a null session is established before any custom URL converter executes.
Custom URL converters can access `flask.session` and session-backed proxies during value conversion.
Requests that previously failed during converter execution because session state was missing now continue through normal route matching.
Routing-derived request metadata is no longer implicitly available during session loading unless matched separately.
acceptance_criteria: When a route uses a custom URL converter that reads `flask.session`, handling a request should not fail because the session is unset.
When a custom URL converter consults session-backed authentication state such as the current user, the converter should see initialized session data during URL matching.
When the session interface does not return a session object, route matching should still execute with a null session available to converter logic.
When session loading is in progress, application code should not assume that endpoint or other routing-derived request information has already been resolved automatically.

task_7.title: Fix nested blueprint prefix composition
task_7.description: Nested Flask blueprints should preserve and combine their effective URL prefixes when they are registered inside other blueprints, so child routes mount at the expected paths whether prefixes are declared on the blueprint itself or supplied during registration. The nested registration should also carry forward the effective registered blueprint name for derived namespaces.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that nested blueprints preserve and combine parent and child URL prefixes correctly, including when a prefix is declared on a Blueprint instance instead of only being passed during registration. Ensure that nested registrations also use the effective registered blueprint name for derived nested namespaces.

expectation.grounded: When a blueprint registers another blueprint, the child's effective `url_prefix` should be resolved from nested registration options first and otherwise from the child blueprint's own `url_prefix`. If both the parent registration state and the child provide a prefix, the mounted prefix should be the slash-normalized concatenation of parent then child. If only one side provides a prefix, that prefix should be used as-is. Nested registration should propagate the effective registered blueprint name to child `name_prefix` handling and to default CLI group naming derived from the blueprint registration name.
expectation.conceptual: Nested blueprints should mount child routes under the full expected path instead of dropping configured prefixes. Renaming a blueprint at registration time should stay consistent for nested endpoint and default CLI namespaces.

constraints.grounded: Do not change behavior for non-nested blueprints. Do not require callers to move `url_prefix` values from `Blueprint(...)` into `register_blueprint(...)`. Preserve slash normalization when joining prefixes, avoid replacing a defined child prefix with an empty value, and continue to allow nested registration with no prefix at either level.
constraints.conceptual: Existing single-blueprint usage should continue to work, and nested prefix handling should be additive and non-destructive. The update should only change cases where nesting previously ignored effective prefixes or inherited names.

behavior: A child blueprint nested under a parent blueprint now inherits the parent's resolved URL prefix during registration.
A child blueprint's own `url_prefix` declared on the `Blueprint` object is now honored when the blueprint is nested, even if the nested `register_blueprint` call does not override it.
When both parent and child prefixes are present, the resulting mounted route prefix is the normalized combination of the two in parent-to-child order.
When only one of the parent or child prefixes is present, that single prefix determines the mounted path instead of falling back to the application root.
Nested endpoint and default CLI namespace derivation follow the effective registered blueprint name rather than only the blueprint object's original name.
acceptance_criteria: When a parent blueprint with `url_prefix='/parent'` nests a child blueprint with `url_prefix='/child'`, a child route registered at `'/'` should be reachable at `/parent/child/`.
When either the parent or child prefix is supplied through `register_blueprint(..., url_prefix=...)` instead of the blueprint constructor, nested routes should still resolve to the combined path.
When only the parent has a prefix, nested child routes should be mounted under that parent path rather than at `/`.
When only the child has a prefix, nested child routes should remain mounted under that child path rather than losing the prefix during nesting.
When a blueprint is registered under a custom name and contains nested blueprints, nested endpoint and default CLI namespace resolution should reflect the effective registered name.

task_9.title: Restore deprecated Config.from_json compatibility
task_9.description: Flask 2.0.1 restores the deprecated Config.from_json API that was removed too early in 2.0.0, so existing applications can continue loading JSON configuration during the deprecation window while receiving a warning to migrate to Config.from_file.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to 2.0.1 can still call the deprecated `Config.from_json()` / `app.config.from_json()` API without runtime breakage, and that its continued availability clearly signals that callers should migrate to `Config.from_file()` rather than treating the API as fully supported again.

expectation.grounded: `Config.from_json(filename, silent=False)` must be available on `Config` in 2.0.1. Calling it should emit a `DeprecationWarning`, load configuration through `Config.from_file` using the Flask JSON loader, preserve the `silent` behavior for missing files, and return the same boolean success signal as the delegated file-loading path.
expectation.conceptual: The JSON config helper should remain usable for one more release as a deprecated compatibility API. Existing code that still loads configuration from JSON through `from_json()` should work again, but callers should receive a deprecation warning and be guided toward `from_file()`.

constraints.grounded: Do not keep `Config.from_json` removed in 2.0.1. Its restored behavior must remain deprecated, continue honoring relative or absolute filenames accepted by the config loader, and match the observable loading and missing-file semantics of the JSON-based `Config.from_file` path rather than introducing different parsing or error behavior.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should restore compatibility without reversing the deprecation decision. It should behave like the existing file-based JSON configuration flow, preserve expected handling of missing files when silence is requested, and avoid new behavior differences beyond re-enabling the deprecated entry point.

behavior: `Config.from_json` is present again in version 2.0.1 instead of being absent at runtime.
Calling `Config.from_json` emits a `DeprecationWarning` rather than failing silently or behaving like a fully supported long-term API.
`Config.from_json` loads JSON configuration through the same file-based config loading flow used by `Config.from_file` with a JSON loader.
The `silent` argument continues to control whether a missing configuration file is ignored.
The method returns the boolean outcome of the underlying configuration load operation.
acceptance_criteria: When an application upgraded to 2.0.1 calls `app.config.from_json(...)`, it should no longer fail because the method is missing.
When `Config.from_json` is called with a valid JSON config file, it should populate configuration values and emit a `DeprecationWarning`.
When `Config.from_json` is called with `silent=True` and the target file does not exist, it should ignore the missing file according to the existing silent-loading contract.
When `Config.from_json` completes, it should report success or failure using the same boolean result semantics as the underlying file-loading API.

task_10.title: Preserve decorator typing and validate blueprint route registration
task_10.description: Version 2.0.1 improves decorator-based typing so registered Flask callables retain their specific signatures in static analysis, and it hardens blueprint route registration by rejecting invalid dotted endpoint or view-function names with regular runtime validation while forwarding explicit automatic OPTIONS configuration.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask's decorator-based registration APIs preserve the decorated function's type information for strict static analysis, and ensure that blueprint route registration exposes consistent runtime validation and option forwarding for invalid endpoint names and automatic OPTIONS handling.

expectation.grounded: Decorator factories such as `errorhandler`, `template_filter`, `template_test`, `template_global`, `app_template_filter`, `app_template_test`, and `app_template_global` should preserve the wrapped callable's specific type instead of degrading it to an untyped callable. Functions decorated through these APIs should remain type-checkable with their original signatures and return types. `Blueprint.add_url_rule` should accept `provide_automatic_options`, forward it during registration, and raise `ValueError` if the provided `endpoint` or the `view_func` name contains a dot character.
expectation.conceptual: Applications upgrading to 2.0.1 should get accurate typing from Flask's decorator APIs so registered handlers, filters, tests, and globals remain statically typed after decoration. Blueprint route registration should also fail predictably for invalid dotted names and continue to honor explicit automatic OPTIONS configuration.

constraints.grounded: The change must not alter the callable object returned by these decorators beyond preserving its type information. Valid blueprint endpoint names and view function names without dots must continue to register normally. Route registration through blueprints must remain a side-effecting registration API, and explicit `provide_automatic_options` values must propagate without changing other route options.
constraints.conceptual: Existing valid decorator usage should keep working the same way while becoming better typed. Valid blueprint routes must continue to register unchanged, and only invalid dotted names should be rejected with a regular runtime validation error. Any explicit automatic OPTIONS setting supplied during blueprint registration must still take effect.

behavior: Decorating an error handler no longer causes the decorated function to lose its concrete callable type in static analysis.

Decorating template filters, template tests, and template globals through the application or a blueprint preserves the decorated callable's type instead of collapsing it to a generic untyped callable.
Registering a blueprint URL rule with an `endpoint` containing `.` raises `ValueError` at registration time.
Registering a blueprint URL rule whose `view_func` name contains `.` raises `ValueError` at registration time.
`Blueprint.add_url_rule` accepts an explicit `provide_automatic_options` argument and forwards it when the rule is registered.
acceptance_criteria: When an application defines a function and decorates it with `errorhandler`, a strict static type checker should still see the function's declared signature and return type after decoration.

When an application or blueprint decorates a callable with `template_filter`, `template_test`, `template_global`, `app_template_filter`, `app_template_test`, or `app_template_global`, the decorated callable should remain specifically typed rather than becoming an untyped callable.
When `Blueprint.add_url_rule` is called with a valid endpoint and a view function name that do not contain dots, the rule should register as before.
When `Blueprint.add_url_rule` is called with an endpoint containing a dot, it should fail immediately with `ValueError`.
When `Blueprint.add_url_rule` is called with a view function whose name contains a dot, it should fail immediately with `ValueError`.
When `Blueprint.add_url_rule` is called with `provide_automatic_options` set explicitly, that setting should be preserved in the resulting route registration.

task_12.title: Support unique names for repeated blueprint registration
task_12.description: Flask 2.0.1 fixes blueprint registration so the same blueprint can be mounted multiple times under distinct registration names, allowing endpoint generation and relative url_for resolution to target the correct mount. The update also makes blueprint name collisions explicit, deprecates re-registering the same blueprint under the same name, and ensures nested blueprints inherit distinct dotted names and composed URL prefixes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that blueprint registration supports mounting the same blueprint more than once with distinct names so endpoint resolution and relative url generation target the correct mount. Ensure that blueprint name collisions are handled explicitly instead of silently reusing the wrong registration. Ensure that nested blueprints keep distinct dotted endpoint names and correct URL prefixes when registered through parent blueprints.

expectation.grounded: Flask.register_blueprint and Blueprint.register_blueprint should accept a name option that overrides the blueprint's pre-dotted registration name for that registration. Endpoints created during registration should use the resolved registration name, including any parent name prefix, so url_for and request endpoint resolution distinguish multiple mounts of the same blueprint and nested blueprints. Registering a different Blueprint object under an already-resolved blueprint name should raise ValueError. Registering the same Blueprint object multiple times under the same resolved name should emit a deprecation warning. A blueprint must not be allowed to register itself as a nested blueprint.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to mount one blueprint in more than one place as long as each mount has its own public registration name. URL generation and endpoint identity should follow the mount that handled the request, including for nested blueprints. Name conflicts should fail fast, repeated reuse of the same name for the same blueprint should be flagged as deprecated, and invalid self-nesting should be rejected.

constraints.grounded: Changing the registration name must not alter the blueprint's declared routes other than the endpoint namespace used for registration. Nested blueprint registration must preserve dotted endpoint naming across parent and child registrations and must compose parent and child url_prefix values when both are provided, while still honoring whichever prefix is defined when only one side provides it. Existing first-registration behavior for one-time blueprint setup should remain tied to whether the Blueprint object has been registered before, not whether a new alias name is used.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must isolate blueprint mounts by name without changing their route definitions beyond public endpoint naming. Nested registrations must remain stable and predictable across parent-child combinations, and the update must avoid introducing duplicate-name ambiguity or accidental recursive blueprint registration.

behavior: A blueprint registration can supply a custom name that becomes the registration-time endpoint namespace used for routes created from that blueprint.
Registering the same blueprint multiple times with different names produces distinct endpoint namespaces, allowing relative and absolute url generation to resolve to the correct mount.
Nested blueprints inherit the resolved parent registration name as a dotted prefix so child endpoints remain unique even when similar blueprint names are reused elsewhere.
When both parent and child blueprints define URL prefixes, the registered child routes use the composed parent and child prefix; when only one prefix is defined, that prefix is used.
Registering a different blueprint under a resolved name that is already in use raises ValueError instead of allowing the collision.
Registering the same blueprint again under the same resolved name emits a deprecation warning indicating that this reuse will become an error in a future release.
Attempting to register a blueprint on itself raises ValueError.
acceptance_criteria: When the same blueprint is registered twice with different name values, it should expose distinct endpoint namespaces and url_for should be able to target each mount independently.

When a request is handled by one mount of a repeatedly registered blueprint, any relative url generation from that mount should resolve within that mount's endpoint namespace rather than another registration of the same blueprint.

When a parent blueprint containing a child blueprint is registered under different names, the child endpoints should use dotted names derived from the parent's resolved registration name and remain distinct across mounts.

When parent and child URL prefixes are both configured, the child routes should be reachable under the combined prefix; when only one side provides a prefix, route registration should still use the available prefix correctly.
When a different blueprint instance is registered with a name that is already resolved to another blueprint, registration should fail with ValueError.
When the same blueprint instance is registered again with the same resolved name, registration should emit a deprecation warning rather than silently treating the registrations as equivalent.
When a blueprint is asked to register itself as a child blueprint, registration should fail with ValueError.

task_13.title: Broaden and refine stream_with_context type hints
task_13.description: The 2.0.1 update improves the public type annotations for `stream_with_context` so that static type checkers accept ordinary iterators, including byte-stream iterators commonly passed to `Response`, and preserve the iterator element type in the returned value. This is a developer-facing typing fix rather than a runtime behavior change.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `stream_with_context` accepts standard iterators used for streaming responses, including iterators yielding bytes or text, without static type errors, while preserving the streamed item type in its public API contract.

expectation.grounded: `stream_with_context` should publicly accept either an `Iterator` yielding string or bytes values, or a callable that returns such an iterator. Its annotated return type should also be an `Iterator` preserving the same yielded text or byte type rather than requiring a generator-specific type.
expectation.conceptual: `stream_with_context` should be typed to work with normal streaming iterators, not only generator objects, so developers can pass existing byte or text iterators to response streaming APIs without type-checking friction.

constraints.grounded: This update should remain limited to the API's typing contract: existing runtime behavior of `stream_with_context` must remain unchanged, direct iterator inputs and callable-produced iterators must both stay supported, and the contract must continue to represent streamed text and streamed bytes accurately.
constraints.conceptual: The change should improve compatibility with static typing tools without changing how streaming works at runtime or narrowing the kinds of stream sources developers can already use.

behavior: `stream_with_context` now advertises support for generic iterators of streamed values instead of only generator instances.
The accepted streamed value type is explicitly modeled as text or bytes, matching common response streaming usage.
Callables that produce streaming iterators remain part of the supported API contract.
The annotated return value is an iterator whose element type matches the input stream's element type.
The update affects static typing and developer ergonomics only, with no intended runtime behavior change.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer passes an existing iterator of bytes to `stream_with_context`, the public type contract should treat that usage as valid.
When a developer passes an existing iterator of text to `stream_with_context`, the public type contract should treat that usage as valid.
When a developer passes a callable that returns a streaming iterator, the public type contract should continue to allow that form.
When `stream_with_context` wraps a bytes or text stream, its documented/annotated return type should remain an iterator of the same yielded value type.
Upgrading from 2.0.0 to 2.0.1 should not require runtime behavior changes in applications that already stream responses through `stream_with_context`.

task_11.title: Fix nested blueprint naming and registration collisions
task_11.description: Version 2.0.1 changes blueprint registration so nested blueprints use fully qualified dotted registration names instead of colliding on their local blueprint name. This enables repeated or nested blueprint usage with distinct namespaces, keeps request and URL generation behavior aligned with the registered name hierarchy, and makes invalid self-registration or ambiguous name reuse surface explicitly.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that nested blueprints are registered and resolved by their full dotted registration name so applications can nest blueprints with the same local name in different places without collisions. Ensure that blueprint registrations can be given a unique registration name when mounted multiple times, while invalid self-registration and ambiguous name conflicts are surfaced predictably.

expectation.grounded: Blueprint registration through Flask.register_blueprint and Blueprint.register_blueprint should use the registered dotted name, including any parent registration path and any registration-time name override, as the namespace for endpoints and other blueprint-scoped behavior. The name option should allow changing the pre-dotted registered name so the same blueprint can be mounted more than once with distinct url_for namespaces. request.blueprint should expose the registered dotted blueprint name for the matched endpoint, and request.blueprints should expose the current registered blueprint path through its parents. Registering a different blueprint under an already-used registered name should raise ValueError, re-registering the same blueprint under the same registered name should emit a deprecation warning, and registering a blueprint on itself should raise ValueError.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to mount nested blueprints with duplicate local names as long as their full registration paths are different. When a blueprint is mounted multiple times, callers should be able to assign distinct registration names so routing and URL generation remain unambiguous. Blueprint-specific request hooks, error handling, URL generation helpers, and request metadata should follow the active registered blueprint hierarchy, and invalid naming conflicts should be rejected or warned about in a consistent way.

constraints.grounded: Existing behavior for uniquely named top-level blueprints must continue to work. Blueprint-scoped resolution must remain tied to the registered namespace rather than the blueprint object's original creation name. Parent and child URL prefixes must still compose correctly across constructor defaults and registration options. The system must not allow recursive self-registration or silent reuse of an ambiguous registered name for a different blueprint.
constraints.conceptual: The update must preserve normal blueprint behavior for existing non-conflicting registrations while removing ambiguity from nested and repeated registrations. Nested routes should still appear at the expected combined URL prefixes, and applications should not silently end up with conflicting blueprint namespaces.

behavior: Nested blueprint endpoints are namespaced under the full dotted registration path rather than only the child blueprint's local name.
Different nested blueprints that share the same local blueprint name can coexist when they are registered under different parent paths.

A registration-time name override changes the blueprint's registered namespace before parent-child dotted names are built, affecting endpoint names and url_for resolution for that registration and its descendants.

Blueprint-scoped features that resolve by blueprint name, including request hooks, error handlers, template context processors, URL default functions, and URL value preprocessors, follow the active registered blueprint hierarchy.
request.blueprint returns the matched blueprint's registered dotted name, and request.blueprints returns the matched blueprint path together with its parent blueprint names.
Registering a blueprint on itself raises ValueError.
Registering a different blueprint under an already-used registered name raises ValueError, while re-registering the same blueprint under the same registered name emits a deprecation warning.
Parent and child URL prefixes continue to compose for nested blueprints whether prefixes are provided at blueprint creation time or at registration time.
acceptance_criteria: When an application registers nested blueprints that have the same local name under different parents, registration should succeed and each nested route should expose a distinct dotted endpoint namespace.

When the same blueprint is mounted multiple times with different registration names, requests to each mount should resolve to different endpoint names and remain addressable through url_for without collisions.

When a nested route is handled inside parent and child blueprints, blueprint-scoped hooks, processors, and error handling should resolve using the active registered blueprint hierarchy rather than only the blueprint's original local name.
When code reads request.blueprint during a matched nested request, it should receive the registered dotted blueprint name for that route.
When code reads request.blueprints during a matched nested request, it should receive the current blueprint path and its parent blueprint names.
When a different blueprint is registered using a registered name that is already in use, registration should fail with ValueError.
When the same blueprint is registered again using the same registered name, registration should emit a deprecation warning instead of silently creating an indistinguishable duplicate.
When parent and child URL prefixes are set on the blueprint definitions, the registration calls, or both, the nested route should remain reachable under the combined prefix.
